steps.label: Do Now: Packets (1 of 2)
steps.content:
Do Now: Packets (1 of 2)

Think → Pair → ShareWhy does sending an image as many small packets help if one is lost?Show the answer

Only the lost packet is sent again, not the whole image. That saves time on the network.

From 2.1 L1. Parts (a) and (b): Cambridge IGCSE 0478/11, November 2025, Question 2(b)(i) and (ii). An employee sends images of houses to his company. The image data is broken down into packets to be sent across a network to the company. The destination internet protocol (IP) address is read by a device in the network. The device uses the IP address to forward the packet towards its correct destination.

Total: 3 marks

steps.text: A similar question. Name the part of a packet that holds the data being sent.
steps.visual: Part 1: at the startPart 2: in the middlePart 3: at the end

steps.text: A packet has three parts. The data being sent is the main load, so it is the biggest part, in the middle.
steps.visual: Part 1: at the startPart 2: in the middlePart 3: at the end

steps.text: The middle part is called the payload. One word is enough for the mark.
For part (b), ask: which part must a device read first, before anything else? An address is needed first.
Name the device. Picture one packet crossing the internet. It meets a junction, then another.
steps.visual: Sender→?→?→Company

steps.text: At every junction, a device reads the destination address and picks the next path for the packet: its route. The device is named after that job.
steps.visual: Sender→picks the route→Company

steps.text: Why? A different case: a family moves house. Their boxes go in three vans, and each van takes its own road.
steps.visual:
Van 1: the main road
Van 2: the coast road
Van 3: the hill road

steps.text: Each driver only sees the boxes in that van. Think: what must be written on every box, and why? Use the same idea for part (c).

steps.label: Do Now: Echo Check (2 of 2)
steps.content:
Do Now: Echo Check (2 of 2)

Think → Pair → ShareWhy check an image after it is sent at all?Show the answer

Interference can change bits on the way. A changed bit can spoil part of the picture.

From 2.2 L3. Part (a): adapted from Cambridge IGCSE 0478/11, November 2025, Question 2(d). An echo check is used to check for errors after the image has been transmitted.

Total: 5 marks

walkthrough.title: Walk me through it: the echo check

steps.text: A similar question. Describe how a checksum detects errors. Answer in the order things happen.
Before sending: the sender calculates a value from the data. The value is sent with the data.
steps.visual: Before sending→After arriving→Decide

steps.text: After arriving: the receiver calculates the value from the data it got.
steps.visual: Before sending→After arriving→Decide

steps.text: Decide: the two values are compared. Different values mean an error. One mark for each step.
steps.visual: Before sending→After arriving→Decide

steps.text: For part (a), use the same three steps for an echo check: what is sent, where it goes next, and who decides.
Why slower? A different case: a parity check adds 1 bit to every 7 bits of data.
steps.visual: 7 data bits + 1 parity bit = 8 bits

steps.text: More bits to send means sending takes a little longer. For part (b), count how far the data travels in an echo check.
steps.visual: more to send = more time

steps.text: Who decides? A different case: you lend a friend a book. Later your friend gives you a book. Is it yours?
steps.visual:
You lend: a clean book
You get: a book with a torn page

steps.text: Only you remember your own book. For part (c), ask: in an echo check, who still holds the data as it was at the start?

steps.label: Symmetric Encryption
steps.content:
2.3 Encryption

Symmetric Encryption

Year 10

  • Today: why data is encrypted when it is sent, and how one shared key locks and unlocks it.
  • You already know: packets, routers and the error checks. They make sure data arrives without errors.
Think → Pair → ShareEvery packet arrives, and every error check passes. Why might the data still not be safe?Show the answer

The packets passed through many devices on the way. Someone could have copied and read them. An error check cannot tell.

steps.label: Data Can Be Intercepted
steps.content:
Data Can Be Intercepted

Think → Pair → SharePredict: Ana sends Ben a message. Every packet arrives with no errors. Could anyone else have read it? Why?Show the worked answer

Yes. The packets passed through routers and cables that Ana does not own. Anyone with access to them could copy the packets on the way.

This is interception. The packets still arrive, so Ana and Ben cannot tell.

  • Packets pass through many devices on the way: routers, cables, Wi-Fi.
  • Someone on the route can intercept the data: copy it and read it.
  • Error checks find changed data. They cannot tell if data was read.
  • Encryption does not stop interception. It makes intercepted data meaningless.
Ana's computer→Router→Router→Ben's computer
Eve copies every packet on the way
Ben: all packets arrived, no errors

steps.label: Plain Text, Key and Cipher Text
steps.content:
Plain Text, Key and Cipher Text

Think → Pair → SharePredict: every letter of MEET AT TEN moves 3 places along the alphabet. Eve intercepts the result. Why can she not understand it?Show the worked answer

She sees PHHW DW WHQ. It is meaningless to her.

To read it she must know how far each letter moved. That number is the key, and she does not have it.

  • Plain text: the data before it is encrypted.
  • The encryption algorithm uses a key to scramble the plain text.
  • Cipher text: the encrypted data. It is meaningless without the key.
  • Decrypt: turn cipher text back into plain text.
Plain textMEET AT TEN
Shiftforward 3
Cipher textPHHW DW WHQ

Algorithm: move each letter forward along the alphabet.
Key: 3. After Z, carry on from A.

steps.label: Exam Question: Why Encrypt?
steps.content:
Exam Question: Why Encrypt?

Think → Pair → ShareWhy does the mark scheme ask what happens IF the data is intercepted?Show the answer

Encryption does not stop the data being copied. So think about what a copy is worth to the person who took it.

Part (a): Cambridge IGCSE 0478/12, March 2024, Question 7(a)(i). Data is transmitted using the internet. The data is encrypted before transmission. Part (b): Cambridge IGCSE 0478/12, June 2026, Question 4(c)(iii).

Total: 3 marks

steps.label: Symmetric Encryption: One Shared Key
steps.content:
Symmetric Encryption: One Shared Key

Think → Pair → SharePredict: Ben receives PHHW DW WHQ. He knows the key is 3. How does he get the message back? Why does that work?Show the worked answer

He moves each letter back 3 places: P to M, H to E, W to T. He reads MEET AT TEN.

Moving back 3 undoes moving forward 3. The same key that encrypted the message decrypts it.

  • In symmetric encryption, the same key encrypts and decrypts.
  • The sender and the receiver both have this key. It is a shared key.
  • Encrypt: move forward by the key. Decrypt: move back by the same key.
  • Everyone can know the algorithm. Only the key is kept secret.
Cipher textPHHW DW WHQ
Shiftback 3
Plain textMEET AT TEN
Ana: key 3→cipher text→Ben: key 3

Same key at both ends.

steps.label: Compare: The Right Key and the Wrong Key
steps.content:
Compare: The Right Key and the Wrong Key

Think → Pair → ShareBen and Eve both get KHOOR. Ben has the key, 3. Eve knows the algorithm and guesses 5. Predict what each one reads. Why?Show the answer

Ben reads HELLO. Eve gets FCJJM: meaningless.

Knowing the algorithm is not enough. Only the right key undoes the shift.

Ben: key 3

Cipher textKHOOR
Shiftback 3
ResultHELLO

The message

Eve: key 5

Cipher textKHOOR
Shiftback 5
ResultFCJJM

Meaningless

  • Same algorithm, different key: a different result.
  • Only the key used to encrypt gives back the plain text.

steps.label: Check: Encrypt and Decrypt
steps.content:
Check: Encrypt and Decrypt

Think → Pair → ShareWhy must Ben move back by exactly the key, not a number close to it?Show the answer

Any other number gives different letters. Only the same key undoes the shift.

Use the alphabet. After Z, carry on from A.

ABCDEFGHIJKLM
NOPQRSTUVWXYZ
Total: 3 marks

steps.label: Activity 1: Encrypt, Decrypt, Crack
steps.content:
Activity 1: Encrypt, Decrypt, Crack

Think → Pair → ShareBen decrypts with the key and gets the message back every time. Why does moving back by the key always work?Show the answer

Encrypting moved every letter forward by the key. Moving back by the same number undoes each move exactly.

Encrypt and decrypt with the key. Then be Eve: no key, only cipher text. New words and keys every time. Stuck? Switch on I need help.

steps.label: Compare: 25 Keys and a 128-Bit Key
steps.content:
Compare: 25 Keys and a 128-Bit Key

Think → Pair → ShareEve has no key, so she tries every key. Predict: why does that work on the letter shift, but not on a key 128 bits long?Show the answer

The letter shift has only 25 keys. A computer tries them all in under a second.

A 128-bit key has 2128 possible keys. Trying them all would take far longer than anyone could wait.

Letter shift

Possible keys: 25
At a billion tries a second:
under a second

Cracked

128-bit key

Possible keys: 340 282 366 920 938 463 463 374 607 431 768 211 456
At a billion tries a second:
more than 10 000 000 000 000 000 000 000 years

Safe

  • Each extra bit in the key doubles the number of possible keys: 1 bit 2 keys, 2 bits 4, 8 bits 256.
  • More possible keys means more to try, so a longer key is harder to crack.

steps.label: Exam Question: The Encryption Key
steps.content:
Exam Question: The Encryption Key

Think → Pair → ShareWhy is the key kept secret, but not the algorithm?Show the answer

Without the key, knowing the algorithm does not help: you would still have to try every key.

Part (a): Cambridge IGCSE 0478/13, June 2026, Question 2(e)(ii). All data that is transmitted across the network is encrypted before transmission. Part (b): Cambridge IGCSE 0478/12, June 2026, Question 4(c)(i). The data that is transmitted is encrypted.

Total: 3 marks

steps.label: The Weak Point: Sharing the Key
steps.content:
The Weak Point: Sharing the Key

Think → Pair → SharePredict: Ben needs the key before he can decrypt. Ana emails it to him. Eve intercepts that email. What can Eve now do? Why?Show the worked answer

Eve can decrypt every message that uses that key. Symmetric encryption uses the same key to encrypt and decrypt, so whoever has the key can read the data.

  • Ben needs the same key before he can decrypt.
  • A key sent across a network can be intercepted, like any other data.
  • Anyone with the key can decrypt the cipher text.
  • So the hard part is sharing the key safely.
  • Next lesson: a method where the key that decrypts is never sent.
Ana→cipher text key 3→Ben
Eve intercepts both
cipher text→key 3→the message

steps.label: Compare: Key Sent and Key Agreed First
steps.content:
Compare: Key Sent and Key Agreed First

Think → Pair → ShareAna sends the same cipher text both times. Predict: in which case can Eve read the message? Why?Show the answer

Left: Eve has the cipher text and the key, so she can decrypt it.

Right: Eve has only the cipher text. Without the key it stays meaningless.

Key sent in the same email

Ana emails the cipher text and the key.
Eve intercepts: cipher text + key
She moves each letter back by the key.

Eve reads it

Key agreed in person first

Ana and Ben met last week and agreed the key.
Eve intercepts: cipher text only
She has no key to undo the shift.

Meaningless to Eve

  • The encryption was the same both times. Only the key sharing was different.

steps.label: Activity 2: Send a Secret Message
steps.content:
Activity 2: Send a Secret Message

Think → Pair → ShareEve copies every packet on the way. Which one does she want most? Why?Show the answer

The packet with the key. With the key and the cipher text, she can decrypt the whole message.

Write a message. Choose a key and press Encrypt. Then choose the person next to you and press Send.

steps.label: Activity 2: Read Your Messages
steps.content:
Activity 2: Read Your Messages

Think → Pair → ShareWhy must the packets go back in order before you decrypt?Show the answer

Each payload is one part of the cipher text. In the wrong order the letters are mixed up, so decrypting gives nonsense.

Tap the packets in order, packet 1 first, and press Check the order. Then move each letter back by the key and type the message.

steps.label: Exam Question: Which Statement Is Correct?
steps.content:
Exam Question: Which Statement Is Correct?

Think → Pair → ShareWhy does encryption not stop Eve copying the packets?Show the answer

The packets still pass through routers and cables she can reach. Encryption changes what the data looks like, not where it goes.

Choose one answer for each.

items.prompt: Cambridge IGCSE 0478/11, November 2025, Question 2(e)(i). The image data is encrypted using symmetric encryption. Which is the correct statement about symmetric encryption?
options: Encrypted text is known as plain text.
The most secure form of encryption.
The encryption key is shared with any device receiving the encrypted data.
items.explain: The receiver decrypts with the same key, so it must be shared. Encrypted text is cipher text, and one key is used, not two.

items.prompt: Eve intercepts cipher text made with symmetric encryption. She knows the algorithm. What else does she need to read it?
options: The key used to encrypt it
items.explain: The same key encrypts and decrypts. With the key, she can turn the cipher text back into plain text.

steps.label: Activity 3: Who Can Read It?
steps.content:
Activity 3: Who Can Read It?

Think → Pair → ShareWhy does Eve need BOTH the cipher text and the key?Show the answer

The cipher text alone is meaningless. The key alone has nothing to unlock.

Read how Ana shares the key and what Eve intercepts. Can Eve read the message? Then explain why, and find the safest way to share the key.

steps.label: Exam Question: How Symmetric Encryption Works (1 of 2)
steps.content:
Exam Question: How Symmetric Encryption Works (1 of 2)

Think → Pair → SharePart (i) has 4 marks. What happens at the sender, and what happens at the receiver?Show the answer

Each mark is one step or one fact. Start at the sender, follow the data to the receiver, and say what each one needs.

Cambridge IGCSE 0478/12, June 2024, Question 2(c)(i). Data is often encrypted when it is transmitted from one device to another.

items.prompt: (i) Explain how data is encrypted using symmetric encryption. [4]
scheme: Data is encrypted and decrypted using the same key
Plain text is encrypted into cipher text (accept cipher text is decrypted into plain text)
Data is encrypted using an algorithm
The key can be generated using an algorithm
The key is transmitted to the receiver
items.guidance: Award 1 mark for: data is encrypted and decrypted using the same key (point 1). Then any three from the other points, up to 3 more marks. Point 4 follows on from point 3: the mark scheme writes them as "data is encrypted using an algorithm ... that uses a key".
items.modelAnswer: One mark: data is encrypted and decrypted using the same key. Then any three from: plain text is encrypted into cipher text, or cipher text is decrypted into plain text; data is encrypted using an algorithm that uses a key; the key can be generated using an algorithm; the key is transmitted to the receiver.

steps.label: Exam Question: How Symmetric Encryption Works (2 of 2)
steps.content:
Exam Question: How Symmetric Encryption Works (2 of 2)

Think → Pair → ShareWhy is "to stop hackers" not the best answer here?Show the answer

Encryption cannot stop anyone copying the data. Say what it does for data that is copied.

Cambridge IGCSE 0478/12, June 2024, Question 2(c)(ii). Data is often encrypted when it is transmitted from one device to another.

scheme: To help keep the data secure
To make the data meaningless (if it is intercepted)
items.modelAnswer: Any one from: to help keep the data secure; to make the data meaningless (if it is intercepted).

steps.label: Practice: Symmetric Encryption
steps.content:
Practice: Symmetric Encryption

Think → Pair → ShareWhy is a system only as safe as its weakest part?Show the answer

Someone trying to read the data uses the easiest way in. Strong encryption does not help if another part is easy to get past.

Part (a): Cambridge IGCSE 0478/11, November 2022, Question 4(b)(i). Rebekah decides to encrypt the data that she transmits whilst using the Internet. She does this to keep the data safe.

Total: 4 marks

steps.label: Plenary: Symmetric Encryption Drill
steps.content:
Plenary: Symmetric Encryption Drill

Think → Pair → ShareWhy practise with new words and keys every time?Show the answer

If you can encrypt and decrypt any word, you really understand how the key works.

Why data is encrypted, the words, encrypting and decrypting, and why sharing the key is the weak point. Your progress is saved.
